edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἤρκει μὲν οὖν τὰ προειρημένα ἐν τοῖς ἰδίᾳ περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐξετασθεῖσι πρὸς τὰς Κέλσου λέξεις· ἵνα δὲ μὴ δοκῶμεν τόπον τινὰ αὐτοῦ τῆς γραφῆς ὑπερβαίνειν ἑκόντες ὡς μὴ δεδυνημένοι λέγειν πρὸς αὐτὸν, φέρε, εἰ καὶ ταυτολογεῖν μέλλομεν, ἐπὶ τοῦτο ἡμᾶς τοῦ Κέλσου προκαλουμένου, ὅση δύναμις ἐπιτεμώμεθα τὸν λόγον, ἐὰν ἄρα τι ὑποπέσῃ περὶ τῶν αὐτῶν ἢ ἐναργέστερον ἢ καινότερον. φησὶ δὴ παραλιπεῖν ὅσα περὶ τοῦ διδασκάλου Χριστιανοὶ διελέγχονται, οὐ παραλιπών (τι) ὧν ἐδύνατο λέγειν· ὅπερ ἐστὶ φανερὸν ἐκ τῶν ἀνωτέρω αὐτῷ λελεγμένων· ἄλλως δὲ ῥητορικῇ ἐγχειρήσει κατακολουθῶν τὸ τοιοῦτο ποιεῖ. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅτι οὐ διελεγχόμεθα περὶ τοῦ τηλικούτου σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, κἂν δοκῇ ὁ ἐγκαλῶν διελέγχειν, δῆλον ἔσται τοῖς φιλαλήθως καὶ ἐξεταστικῶς ὅλοις τοῖς περὶ αὐτοῦ προφητευομένοις καὶ ἀναγεγραμμένοις ἐντυγχάνουσιν. ἑξῆς δὲ, ἐπεὶ νομίζεται συγχωρητικῶς λέγειν περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος οτι δοκείτω τις ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄγγελος οὗτος εἶναι, φαμὲν ὅτι τοῦτ᾿ οὐχ ὡς συγχωρούμενον ἀπὸ Κέλσου λαμβάνομεν, τῷ δ᾿ ἔργῳ αὐτοῦ ἐνορῶντες ὅλῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδεδημηκότος κατὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ λόγον καὶ τὴν διδασκαλίαν, ὡς ἕκαστος ἐχώρει τῶν προσιεμένων αὐτόν. ὅπερ ἔργον ἦν τοῦ, ὡς ὠνόμασεν ἡ περὶ αὐτοῦ προφητεία, οὐχ ἁπαξαπλῶς ἀγγέλου ἀλλὰ τοῦ τῆς „μεγάλης βουλῆς“ ἀγγέλου· ἤγγελλε γὰρ ἀνθρώποις τὴν μεγάλην τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς τῶν ὅλων περὶ αὐτῶν βουλὴν, εἰκόντων μὲν τῷ βιοῦν ἐν καθαρᾷ θεοσεβείᾳ ὡς ἀναβαινόντων διὰ τῶν μεγάλων πράξεων πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, μὴ προσιεμένων δὲ ὡς ἑαυτοὺς μακρυνόντων ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἀπώλειαν διὰ τῆς περὶ θεοῦ ἀπιστίας ὁδευόντων. εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς φησιν· εἰ καὶ ἄγγελος οὗτος πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ἦλθεν. ἆρα πρῶτος ἧκε καὶ μόνος, ἤ καὶ ἄλλοι πρότερον; καὶ πρὸς ἑκάτερον δὲ διὰ πλειόνων οἴεται ἀπαντᾶν, οὐδενὸς δὴ τῶν ὡς ἀληθῶς Χριστιανῶν λέγοντος μόνον τὸν Χριστὸν ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τῷ (γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων·) καὶ ἄλλους ὦφθαί φησιν ἀνθρώποις ὁ Κέλσος, εἰ μὲν δὴ φαῖεν ὅτι μόνος.
pass_a_gloss: The things said before (προλέγω) in the passages examined separately (ἰδίᾳ ἐξετάζω) about our Saviour Jesus Christ in reply to Celsus's statements (λέξεις) were enough (ἀρκέω); but so that we may not seem to pass over (ὑπερβαίνω) willingly (ἑκών) any place (τόπος) of his writing (γραφή) as not able to speak against him, come (φέρε), even if we are about to repeat ourselves (ταυτολογέω), Celsus calling us forth (προκαλέομαι) to this, as far as is in our power let us cut short (ἐπιτέμνω) the discussion (λόγος), if perhaps something should occur (ὑποπίπτω) about the same things either clearer (ἐναργέστερον) or newer (καινότερον). He says then that he passes over all the things on which Christians are refuted (διελέγχω) about the teacher, not passing over anything of what he could say; which is clear from what was said by him above; but idly (ἄλλως) following (κατακολουθέω) a rhetorical device (ῥητορικὴ ἐγχείρησις) he does such a thing. But also that we are not refuted about so great (τηλικοῦτος) a Saviour of ours, even if the accuser (ἐγκαλέω) seems to refute, will be clear to those who with love of truth (φιλαλήθως) and with examination (ἐξεταστικῶς) read (ἐντυγχάνω) all the things prophesied (προφητεύω) and recorded (ἀναγράφω) about him. Next, since he is thought to say by way of concession (συγχωρητικῶς) about the Saviour that 'let this one seem truly to be an angel', we say that we take this not as conceded (συγχωρέω) by Celsus, but looking into (ἐνοράω) the work (ἔργον) of him who has visited (ἐπιδημέω) the whole race (γένος) of men according to his own word and the teaching, as each of those accepting (προσίεμαι) him had room (χωρέω). Which work was of one not simply (ἁπαξαπλῶς) an angel, but, as the prophecy about him named (ὀνομάζω) him, the angel of 'great counsel' (μεγάλη βουλή); for he announced (ἀγγέλλω) to men the great counsel of the God and Father of all things about them, of those yielding (εἴκω) to living in pure godliness (θεοσέβεια) as ascending (ἀναβαίνω) through the great deeds (πράξεις) to God, and of those not accepting as putting themselves far (μακρύνω) from God and journeying (ὁδεύω) to destruction (ἀπώλεια) through unbelief (ἀπιστία) about God. Then next he says: 'Even if this one came as an angel to men, did he come first and alone, or others too before?' And to each alternative (ἑκάτερον) he thinks to reply (ἀπαντάω) at length, no one of the true Christians saying that Christ alone has visited the (race of men); and Celsus says others too were seen (ὁράω) by men, 'if indeed they should say that he alone'.

pass_b_english: What we said earlier, in the parts where we dealt separately with our Saviour Jesus Christ in reply to Celsus's statements, would have been enough. But so that we may not seem to pass over any passage of his writing on purpose, as though we could not answer it, come, even if we are going to repeat ourselves, since Celsus challenges us to it, let us treat the matter as briefly as we can, and see whether anything clearer or newer on the same matters occurs to us.

He says, then, that he passes over all the points on which Christians are refuted about their teacher, though he has passed over nothing that he could say, as is clear from what he said earlier; he does this merely by following a rhetorical device. But that we are not refuted about so great a Saviour as ours, even if our accuser seems to refute us, will be clear to those who read closely, with a love of truth, all that was prophesied and recorded about him.

Next, since he is thought to be speaking by way of concession when he says of the Saviour, “Let this man be taken to be truly an angel,” we say that we do not take this as something Celsus concedes; we take it from looking at the work of him who has visited the whole human race with his own word and teaching, as far as each of those who received him had room for it. That was the work of one who was not simply an angel but, as the prophecy about him named him, the Angel “of great counsel” (Isaiah 9:6). For he announced to men the great counsel of God, the Father of all things, concerning them: that those who yield to it by living in pure godliness are going up to God through great deeds, while those who do not receive him are putting themselves far from God (Psalm 73:27) and travelling toward destruction through their unbelief concerning God.

Then next he says: “Even if this man came to men as an angel, did he come first and alone, or did others come before him too?” And he thinks he meets each alternative at length, though no one who is truly a Christian says that Christ alone has visited the human race. And Celsus says that others too have appeared to men: “If they should say that he alone …”
notes: Isaiah 9:6 in English Bibles = LXX Isaiah 9:5 (μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος, a reading found only in the Septuagint). Origen plays on ἄγγελος / ἤγγελλε ('angel' / 'announced'); the pun cannot be kept in English. Psalm 73:27 = LXX Psalm 72:27 (οἱ μακρύνοντες ἑαυτοὺς ἀπὸ σοῦ ἀπολοῦνται): ἑαυτοὺς μακρυνόντων ... ἐπὶ τὴν ἀπώλειαν matches both the verb and the outcome, so it is cited as a clear allusion. ὡς ἕκαστος ἐχώρει may echo Matthew 19:11–12 (χωρεῖν) but is not cited. εἰκόντων ... τῷ βιοῦν: τῷ βιοῦν taken as the dative object of εἴκω ('give themselves to living'). The last sentence is broken in the staged text: (γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων·) is an editorial supplement, and καὶ ἄλλους ὦφθαί φησιν ... εἰ μὲν δὴ φαῖεν ὅτι μόνος seems to give Celsus's opening words of his first alternative (compare 5.52), so they are printed as a broken-off quotation. The quoted 'Even if this man came ...' differs slightly from Celsus's wording in 5.52; Origen is restating it. Text has οτι (unaccented) before δοκείτω; read ὅτι introducing the quotation. Review: εἰκόντων ... τῷ βιοῦν is now read as 'yielding (to the counsel) by living', τῷ βιοῦν as dative of means, in contrast with μὴ προσιεμένων ('not receiving'); the earlier note's 'give themselves to living' is withdrawn. τῷ δ᾿ ἔργῳ αὐτοῦ ἐνορῶντες depends on λαμβάνομεν ('we take it from looking at his work'), so the second sentence is joined back to the first. ἐὰν ἄρα τι ὑποπέσῃ: 'and see whether anything ... occurs' (the old 'in case' could read as 'to prevent'). Isaiah 9:6 (LXX 9:5) and Psalm 73:27 (LXX 72:27) checked against the LXX wording.

Open doubt (review): 5.53: the last sentence is broken in the staged text and contains an editorial supplement. The first draft printed it as a broken-off quotation and the review kept that, with a note.
